superdelegates.title: Superdelegates
superdelegates.summary: The Democratic Party's automatic-delegate system, which John Kiriakou describes as created after George McGovern's 1972 landslide loss to return nominating power to party insiders. He cites West Virginia and Wyoming in 2016, where Bernie Sanders won the vote and Hillary Clinton took every delegate, and notes the Republican Party has no equivalent — which is why an insurgent like Donald Trump could win its nomination.
dyk: ...that [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) says superdelegates are why [Bernie Sanders](/wiki/bernie-sanders) could beat Hillary Clinton in both West Virginia and Wyoming in 2016 and still lose literally every delegate from those states?

...that [Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) attributes [Donald Trump](/wiki/donald-trump)'s 2016 nomination partly to a structural asymmetry — the Republican Party has no superdelegates, so an insurgent candidate can actually win it, which he says is *"much less likely to happen"* in the [Democratic Party](/wiki/democratic-party-2025-approval-decline)?
superdelegates.body:
**Superdelegates** are the automatic convention delegates of the U.S. Democratic Party — members of the House and Senate, governors, lieutenant governors, state party directors and state committee chairs, seated by virtue of office rather than by primary vote. [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou), a former Democrat, treats the system as the mechanism by which the party's nominating contests are decided against their own voters.<Cite t="04:06" />

## Origin

Kiriakou dates the system to the aftermath of 1972. Nobody at the DNC had wanted George McGovern as that year's nominee: he was the most popular candidate at the time, especially among young people, but the weakest nationwide, and he went on to lose 49 states. The party let him have the nomination and then, immediately after the defeat, instituted superdelegates.<Cite t="03:35" /><Cite t="04:06" />

Kiriakou's objection is one of first principles — *"it's a party of the people, right? If the people want George McGovern as the nominee, then George McGovern should be the nominee"* — and his reading of the intent is that the party wanted to go back to *"the days with the smoke-filled back rooms with the party bosses choosing who's going to be the nominee."* The efficiency of the design, as he and his interviewer work out between them, is that concentrating the decision in roughly 1,500 automatic delegates leaves far fewer people who need to be controlled.<Cite t="04:06" /><Cite t="05:08" /><Cite t="05:39" />

## West Virginia and Wyoming

The case Kiriakou puts forward as decisive is the 2016 primary, in which [Bernie Sanders](/wiki/bernie-sanders) beat Hillary Clinton in both West Virginia and Wyoming and Clinton took *"literally every delegate"* from those states.<Cite t="04:37" />

He places this alongside the debate-question episode: DNC chair Debbie Wasserman Schultz, he says, gave the Clinton campaign the debate questions in advance, and Sanders did not receive them. His summary is unqualified — *"it's fixed."*<Cite t="09:47" /><Cite t="10:18" />

## The pattern before and after

Kiriakou describes the same treatment applied to other insurgents. Of [Tulsi Gabbard](/wiki/tulsi-gabbard)'s presidential run: every time she inched up in the polls, the DNC changed the rules for participating in the next debate, setting the threshold one or two percentage points out of her reach each time, because her message threatened them and she would not get with the program.<Cite t="03:05" />

Of Jesse Jackson, who won eleven contests in 1988 and had real momentum: Kiriakou says the party let him self-destruct, because he was never a Democratic Party insider and *"the insiders were not going to let him have that nomination."* Asked who the deciding "we" actually is, his answer is the state committee chairs who make up the Democratic National Committee.<Cite t="08:45" /><Cite t="09:15" /><Cite t="09:47" />

## The Republican asymmetry

The Republican Party, Kiriakou notes, has no equivalent system — which is precisely why an insurgent candidate such as [Donald Trump](/wiki/donald-trump) could take its nomination, an outcome he considers *"much less likely to happen"* on the Democratic side.<Cite t="08:45" /><Cite t="09:15" />

## See also

- [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou)
- [Tulsi Gabbard](/wiki/tulsi-gabbard)

george-mcgovern.title: George McGovern
george-mcgovern.summary: The 1972 Democratic presidential nominee, whose landslide defeat John Kiriakou identifies as the pretext for creating superdelegates. As a George Washington University sophomore in 1983, Kiriakou wrote to McGovern offering the campus theater for a campaign launch; McGovern telephoned him personally, announced his 1984 candidacy there, and afterwards took him home for tuna sandwiches made by his wife.
dyk: ...that [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) was a college sophomore when he wrote to George McGovern offering him a campus theater — and McGovern telephoned him personally, then chose the venue to launch his 1984 presidential campaign, later inviting [Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) home for tuna sandwiches?

...that per [Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou), George McGovern's 49-state defeat in 1972 was the pretext the Democratic Party used to create [superdelegates](/wiki/superdelegates) — a system he says has been used against insurgents from Jesse Jackson to [Bernie Sanders](/wiki/bernie-sanders) ever since?
george-mcgovern.body:
**George McGovern** was the Democratic Party's 1972 presidential nominee, defeated in a 49-state landslide. [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) discusses him in two registers: as the occasion for the creation of [superdelegates](/wiki/superdelegates), and as the subject of one of his own formative political memories.<Cite t="03:35" /><Cite t="05:39" />

## The 1984 announcement

In 1983 Kiriakou was a sophomore at George Washington University and — as he puts it — speakers committee chairman and effectively the entire committee of the College Democrats, in the days when he was a Democrat. Reading a short item in the *Washington Post* that McGovern was considering another run, he wrote offering the university's theater and a ready supply of student volunteers.<Cite t="05:39" /><Cite t="06:10" />

McGovern telephoned him a few days later, waking him, and asked to see the theater. He came to campus — nobody recognised him on the walk over — approved the venue, and told Kiriakou not to tell anyone, but that he was going to run for president again. Kiriakou put out the press release; the Marvin Theater was packed and the announcement made the news.<Cite t="06:10" /><Cite t="06:40" />

Kiriakou's account of the guest list is affectionate: McGovern *"brought his own influencers"* — Mo Udall, the Arizona congressman who had run in 1976; the Academy Award-winning actor Cliff Robertson and his wife Dina Merrill; and Frank Mankiewicz, who had been Robert Kennedy Sr.'s press secretary and was serving as McGovern's. After the announcement McGovern shook every hand and then invited Kiriakou back to his apartment, where his wife made tuna sandwiches. *"Just the loveliest people."*<Cite t="07:11" /><Cite t="07:43" />

McGovern finished third in the 1984 contest, behind Walter Mondale and Gary Hart — a result Kiriakou calls crazy given where he had started. He notes that McGovern was pressed continually to drop out, and reads the pressure as being about the constituency he held: *"because he was pulling young people."*<Cite t="07:43" /><Cite t="08:13" />

yalta-conference.title: Yalta conference
yalta-conference.summary: The February 1945 Allied conference, which John Kiriakou uses as his teaching example of what a well-placed spy is worth: Stalin, told by a source inside the White House that Roosevelt was ill, insisted on a venue requiring a punishing multi-leg journey, then refused to delay the talks — and an exhausted Roosevelt, Kiriakou says, conceded Poland in order to go to bed.
dyk: ...that [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) teaches the [Yalta conference](/wiki/yalta-conference) as a lesson in the value of a well-placed spy — Stalin knew from a source inside the White House that Roosevelt was ill, and chose the hardest possible venue to reach?

...that per [Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou), an exhausted Roosevelt gave up Poland at [Yalta](/wiki/yalta-conference) simply to be allowed to go to sleep — and died of a cerebral hemorrhage two months later, a case he cites when explaining what [intelligence](/wiki/cia) is actually for?
yalta-conference.body:
The **Yalta conference** of February 1945 brought Franklin Roosevelt, Winston Churchill and Joseph Stalin together in Crimea to settle the post-war reorganisation of Germany and Europe. [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) uses it as a set-piece illustration of what a single well-placed human source is worth — a question first put to him in the George Washington University class that led to his own recruitment.<Cite t="13:24" /><Cite t="13:54" />

## Why Yalta

Kiriakou's framing begins with the venue: Yalta is *"really, really hard to get to,"* and with the war still on there was no flying over it. He traces Roosevelt's route as a train to Norfolk, Virginia, a sea crossing to Malta taking about a week, then Cairo, then Iran, and only then Yalta.<Cite t="13:54" />

The explanation he gives for that itinerary is intelligence. Stalin had a spy in the White House, and the spy told him Roosevelt was sick; Stalin therefore wanted him as weak as possible when the talks began, and chose accordingly.<Cite t="14:26" />

## The concession

On arrival the American delegation was exhausted and Roosevelt wanted to sleep, but Stalin insisted the talks begin immediately. In Kiriakou's telling the consequence was concrete: *"just to be able to go to bed, Roosevelt gave up Poland."*<Cite t="14:26" /><Cite t="14:56" />

Roosevelt died of a cerebral hemorrhage on 12 April 1945, two months after the conference. Kiriakou's closing question to his interviewer is the point of the whole anecdote: *"do you see what a well-placed spy can do for you?"*<Cite t="15:26" />
